question: Which statement best describes Untrusted input?
options: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted request. Server protections such as SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens help stop it. It is like someone forging an order using a trusted courier. The server must verify that a sensitive action was intentionally requested. In practice, protect a state-changing request on the server even when a cookie is SameSite. In a real page, require a CSRF check for a cookie-authenticated state change.

Text from a user, URL, or outside service may contain content an attacker controls. Display it as text and validate it before sensitive use. It is like reading a note without letting it issue commands. Decide what formats and lengths your application accepts. In practice, render a user’s comment as text instead of concatenating it into an HTML string. In a real page, render comments as text so markup from a user is not interpreted as code.

The same-origin policy limits how one site can read another site’s data. CORS lets a server grant selected cross-origin access; it is not a frontend switch that makes private APIs secure. It is like a receptionist checking which visitors may enter a room. Configure allowed origins on the server and still authenticate users. In practice, allow a trusted origin only when the API needs cross-origin browser access. In a real page, configure CORS on the API server and permit only known origins.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when attacker-controlled content runs as code in a trusted page. Use safe rendering, avoid unsafe HTML insertion, and apply a carefully tested Content Security Policy. It is like preventing a visitor’s note from being treated as an official instruction. Fix the unsafe input path first; a policy is an added defense. In practice, a CSP can limit script sources, but it does not repair unsafe application logic. In a real page, test CSP changes in report-only mode before enforcing a policy that may block needed scripts.
